Rolling-origin backtest

Source: R/eval-backtest.R
mt_backtest.Rd

For each forecast origin, the data are cut at the origin, the preprocessing pipeline and the model are fitted on the training window only, and predictive draws for the next h years are compared with the observations (rolling-origin evaluation; Tashman 2000). Nothing after the origin enters the fit, including ungrouping and smoothing (they are part of prep).

Usage

mt_backtest(
  spec,
  data,
  origins = NULL,
  h = 10,
  prep = NULL,
  n_draws = 200,
  n_origins = 5,
  seed = 1,
  cores = 1,
  score_estimated = FALSE,
  quantities = NULL,
  contrast = NULL
)

Arguments

spec

A model specification.

data

An mt_data object.

origins

Last training years. Default: the last n_origins years whose full horizon h is observed, so that every horizon is scored equally often.

h

Forecast horizon.

prep

Preprocessing pipeline (mt_prep()).

n_draws

Number of draws per origin.

n_origins

Number of origins when origins is NULL.

seed

Random seed (forecast draws and the randomised PIT); NULL for none.

cores

Cores used over origins (forked processes; 1 on Windows).

score_estimated

Score cells whose deaths were estimated (for example suppressed cells filled by mt_fill_suppressed()); by default only observed cells are scored.

quantities

Derived quantities scored in addition to the rates: "life_expectancy" (at the first age of the grid, in years) and/or "asr" (age-standardised rate, European Standard Population 2013, on the log scale; direct standardisation on the age groups of the standard with the exposures of the test year, see asr()), computed from the predictive draws of deaths aggregated to the observed age groups of each stratum and test year, like the observed values. Years whose observed cells do not cover the full age range without gaps (missing, suppressed or estimated cells) are skipped. A zero ASR (no deaths at any age) is replaced by the smallest value that half a death gives. They are added as rows with target "life_expectancy" or "asr"; summarise them with mt_score(..., target = ).

contrast

Optional c(var = , ref = ): a stratum variable and its reference level. With quantities, the differences between every other level and the reference level (with the same values of the other stratum variables) are scored too, path by path: targets "life_expectancy_gap" (difference in years) and "asr_gap" (difference of log ASR, the log rate ratio). This checks forecasts of inequality, whose uncertainty depends on how the paths of the strata move together; the rows carry the stratum of the compared level.

Value

An object of class mt_backtest: a data.table with one row per observed cell, origin and horizon: model, prep (the preprocessing steps, "none" without), origin, horizon, stratum columns, age_lo, age_hi, period, observed (log rate), the MASE scale scale (mean absolute year-to-year change in the training data), target ("rate", or the derived quantity), the forecast median and mean, and the scores crps, wis, ae (absolute error of the median), cov50, cov80, cov95 and pit (randomised for ties), and for the opt-in summaries of mt_score() (measures) the standard deviation of the draws sd, cov90 and the half-widths hw80, hw90 and hw95 of the central intervals. Rows of derived quantities have no age_lo, age_hi and scale. Summarise with mt_score().

Details

Evaluation happens at the resolution of the observed deaths: grid draws of deaths (Poisson given the exposures of the test years, which are treated as known) are summed to each observed cell, so models on single years of age can be scored against data in 5-year groups. Exposures of the test years are ungrouped if needed (no deaths of the test years are used for that).

Data whose deaths were ungrouped beforehand with mt_ungroup(), and data smoothed with mt_smooth(), are refused: the forecasts would be scored against estimates instead of observations, and an ungrouping or smoothing over time has seen the test years. Ungroup or smooth inside each fit instead (prep = mt_prep(step_ungroup()), step_smooth()). With step_regroup(), the test data are summed to the age groups of the fit.

The log rate of an observed cell is log(max(D, 0.5) / E): a cell without deaths counts as half a death, so that its log rate is finite (a convention of this package; reference unknown). The predictive draws of deaths are first summed from the grid to the observed cell and then floored in the same way, so that draws and observations are treated alike; a floor per grid cell would put the draws of a grouped cell with few deaths above the observation.

Strata without forecast draws at an origin (the model failed in them or gave missing rates) are not scored, with a warning of class mt_warning_backtest. Compare models on the cells all of them scored (mt_score_table() does so for mt_compare() results).

Scores (see mt_score() for their summaries): the CRPS is the empirical-CDF estimator from the draws (Grimit et al. 2006), the mean absolute difference between the draws and the observation minus half the mean absolute difference between pairs of draws. It is the CRPS of the empirical distribution of the draws, which exceeds that of the predictive distribution by about E|X - X'| / (2 n_draws) on average, so compare models backtested with the same n_draws. The weighted interval score uses the 23 quantiles of the COVID-19 forecast hubs (Bracher et al. 2021); the PIT is randomised where draws equal the observation (Czado, Gneiting and Held 2009), as with zero deaths.

References

Bracher J, Ray EL, Gneiting T, Reich NG (2021). Evaluating epidemic forecasts in an interval format. PLoS Computational Biology 17(2): e1008618. doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008618

Czado C, Gneiting T, Held L (2009). Predictive model assessment for count data. Biometrics 65(4): 1254-1261.

Gneiting T, Raftery AE (2007). Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation. Journal of the American Statistical Association 102(477): 359-378. doi:10.1198/016214506000001437

Grimit EP, Gneiting T, Berrocal VJ, Johnson NA (2006). The continuous ranked probability score for circular variables and its application to mesoscale forecast ensemble verification. Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society 132: 2925-2942.

Tashman LJ (2000). Out-of-sample tests of forecasting accuracy: an analysis and review. International Journal of Forecasting 16(4): 437-450.

Examples

x <- mt_example(deaths = "single", years = 1990:2012)
bt <- mt_backtest(rwd(), x, origins = c(2005, 2007), h = 5, n_draws = 100)
mt_score(bt)
#>                     model       crps        wis        mae      rmse     mase
#>                    <char>      <num>      <num>      <num>     <num>    <num>
#> 1: Random walk with drift 0.05507087 0.04923878 0.07405228 0.1188856 1.265727
#>        cov50    cov80     cov95  pit_mean     n     unit
#>        <num>    <num>     <num>     <num> <int>   <char>
#> 1: 0.6415493 0.878169 0.9591549 0.4867606  1420 log rate
